items.title: What have we been doing to support the economy during the Covid crisis?
items.description: The Covid (coronavirus) pandemic shook the UK’s economy. We’ve been helping to keep it stable by supporting businesses and jobs.

items.title: Who pays for the Bank of England?
items.description: Although we’re a public body, each year we give around £350 million back to the public through HM Treasury.

items.title: What is the economy?
items.description: An economy is a system for distributing limited resources… confused? Keep reading

items.title: What is capital?
items.description: The financial resources a bank has that act as a cushion against unexpected losses

items.title: How has money changed over time?
items.description: How we pay for things, and even the concept of paying, have developed over 11,000 years.

items.title: What do I need to know about debt?
items.description: Learn more about debt and see how yours compares to the rest of the UK

items.title: What is the Prudential Regulation Authority (PRA)?
items.description: The PRA supervises about 1,300 financial institutions, including banks and insurance companies

items.title: What are cryptoassets (cryptocurrencies)?
items.description: A way of storing value electronically outside of centralised systems and away from regulators.

items.title: How much is a banknote worth?
items.description: While rare serial numbers often generate interest, banknotes will only ever be worth their face value to us.

items.title: What is financial stability?
items.description: A stable financial system is one that can provide essential services to households and businesses in good times and bad.

items.title: Is my money safe from cyber-attacks?
items.description: Cyber-attacks are becoming more frequent and advanced. Here's what you need to know.

items.title: What does insurance cover?
items.description: Insurance provides protection against financial loss for people and companies.

items.title: How do card payments work?
items.description: Whether you’re buying groceries or a laptop, paying by card only takes seconds. Here’s how the money gets from A to B.

items.title: What are interest rates?
items.description: Interest is the cost of borrowing money or the reward for saving

items.title: How is money created?
items.description: Most of the money in the economy is created by banks when they provide loans.

items.title: What is deflation?
items.description: Falling prices are not always cause for celebration.

items.title: Financial market infrastructures – what happens when you pay?
items.description: There’s a network of systems that make payments possible. These are known as financial market infrastructures – or FMIs for short.

items.title: Why are football players paid so much?
items.description: The short answer is: supply and demand.

items.title: Why is competition important in banking?
items.description: We aim to keep banks safe, but of a bit of healthy competition can be a good thing for consumers.

items.title: What risks do banks take?
items.description: The three largest risks banks take are credit risk, market risk and operational risk.

items.title: Why do we regulate banks?
items.description: We want to keep the financial system stable and individual firms safe

items.title: How do we know how much money to print?
items.description: We mostly print money to replace old, worn-out banknotes. But it’s also up to demand.

items.title: What’s the Bank of England’s role in the housing market?
items.description: If we look at how much British households borrow, more than seven out of ten pounds are for mortgages.

items.title: How does the housing market affect the economy?
items.description: House prices affect how much money people spend. They have tripled since the late 1970s.

items.title: Why are new banknotes made of polymer?
items.description: Our new banknotes are made of polymer because it is cleaner, safer and stronger than paper.

items.title: The Bank of England in literature
items.description: We make an appearance in literature as a setting, an institution and even a character in itself.

items.title: Climate change: what are the risks to financial stability?
items.description: Climate change poses risks for the stability of the financial system, particularly for the insurance and banking sectors.

items.title: What is money?
items.description: Feathers, shells and even teeth … money has taken many forms over time

items.title: How fast can the economy grow?
items.description: While we often think of economic growth as good news, it can also happen too rapidly

items.title: Is the global financial system any safer than before?
items.description: There is more work to be done, but the global financial system is safe, simpler and fairer today than it was a decade ago.

items.title: How is the Bank of England independent of the Government?
items.description: We have specific legal responsibilities for setting policy – for interest rates, for financial stability, and for the regulation of banks and insurance companies.

items.title: Why does money depend on trust?
items.description: In the past you could exchange banknotes for gold. Today the value of money comes from trust.

items.title: How will driverless cars affect the economy?
items.description: UK drivers spend 127 hours stuck in traffic each year.
